title: India's Economy Grew 7.8% Last Quarter. The Hard Part Starts Now.
excerpt: Farm output and construction drove a surprise beat over forecasts, but the Iran war, a weak rupee and a subpar monsoon threaten to drag growth below 7% this year.
body:
India's economy delivered a performance that nobody expected — and one that may not last.

The January-March quarter logged GDP growth of 7.8%, the government announced on Friday, blowing past the 7.2% median forecast in a Reuters poll of economists. For the full fiscal year ending in March, the economy expanded 7.7%, up from the 7.6% estimate released in February and well ahead of the 7.1% growth recorded the prior year.

The surprise came from two sectors that rarely dominate headlines: agriculture and construction. Farm output, battered by uneven rains in recent years, staged a meaningful recovery. Construction activity accelerated to 8.4%, buoyed by government capital spending on highways, metro projects and affordable housing. Manufacturing grew 7.3%, slower than the prior year but still solid. Private consumption — the engine that employs the most Indians — rose 7.1%.

## The Numbers Behind the Beat

Gross value added, which strips out volatile indirect taxes and subsidies, grew an even stronger 7.9%. The previous quarter's growth was also revised upward, from 7.8% to 8.0%, meaning the economy was running hotter than anyone realized heading into the new fiscal year.

India's nominal GDP reached ₹346.36 lakh crore ($4.1 trillion at current exchange rates), a figure that underscores the country's sheer scale as the world's fifth-largest economy. The 8.9% growth in nominal terms also suggests pricing power has held up, even as global supply chains remained strained.

For NRIs watching from abroad, the numbers offer reassurance that the Indian economy they send remittances to, invest in, and plan retirements around is not buckling under pressure. Real estate in major metros, a favorite NRI asset class, has been a direct beneficiary of construction momentum and stable interest rates.

## But the Rear-View Mirror Is Misleading

Here is the problem: the January-March quarter caught only the tail end of the Middle East crisis. The U.S.-Iran conflict erupted on February 28, giving the quarter barely a month of disruption to absorb. The full damage has yet to show up in the data.

Hours before the GDP numbers dropped, the Reserve Bank of India laid out a bleaker forward picture. Governor Sanjay Malhotra held the repo rate at 5.25% but revised the inflation forecast sharply higher — to 5.1% from 4.6% — and trimmed the GDP growth forecast for the current fiscal year to 6.6% from 6.9%.

The rupee has fallen nearly 5% this year to historic lows around 95 to the dollar, battered by record foreign fund outflows and crude oil prices hovering near $96 a barrel. India imports over 85% of its crude, and a significant share transits the Strait of Hormuz, which remains partially blockaded.

## Three Risks Converging

Three headwinds are converging that make the next four quarters fundamentally different from the last four.

First, oil. India is the world's third-largest crude importer. With Brent near $96 and the Hormuz disruption showing no signs of resolution, the energy import bill is climbing rapidly. Every $10 increase in crude typically adds 0.3 to 0.4 percentage points to India's current account deficit.

Second, the monsoon. The India Meteorological Department has forecast a below-normal southwest monsoon this year — the worst outlook in 11 years. A weak monsoon pushes up food prices, which account for nearly 40% of India's consumer price index. The RBI is already bracing for food-driven inflation to compound the energy shock.

Third, capital flight. Foreign institutional investors have been net sellers of Indian equities for months, pulling billions out of the market. The RBI's new measures — scrapping capital gains tax for foreign holders of government bonds and sweetening dollar deposit rates for NRIs — are designed to reverse that outflow, but their impact will take time.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

The GDP beat is real, but backward-looking. For NRIs considering investments, remittances, or property purchases, the next six months will be defined by oil prices, monsoon rains and whether the Middle East conflict de-escalates.

The RBI's decision to hold rates rather than hike is a bet that the current shocks are temporary. If that bet is wrong, rate hikes later this year could cool the property market and slow growth further. Oxford Economics warned on Friday that activity has "already started slowing" and the RBI's cautious hold "will not be enough to prevent growth from undershooting."

India is still the fastest-growing major economy in the world. That has not changed. What has changed is the margin of safety around that growth — and for the first time in two years, it is shrinking.

*Sources: Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Reserve Bank of India, Reuters, Wall Street Journal, Morningstar, Oxford Economics*
